title: India Just Lowered Its Foodgrain Production Target for the First Time in Years. El Niño Is the Reason.
excerpt: The government set a target of 373.93 million tonnes for 2026-27 — down from last year's record 376.56 million tonnes — as IMD predicts below-normal monsoon rainfall.
body:
India has set a foodgrain production target of 373.93 million tonnes for the 2026-27 crop year — a rare downward revision from last year's record output of 376.56 million tonnes. The reason: a weakening monsoon forecast that has put the entire kharif season under a cloud.

## The Numbers Behind the Cut

The target includes 151 million tonnes of rice, 121.5 million tonnes of wheat, 28.42 million tonnes of pulses, 18.08 million tonnes of nutri-cereals, and 52.50 million tonnes of maize. The most notable reductions are in rice and maize — the two crops most dependent on monsoon rainfall and the most exposed to El Niño disruption.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast below-normal rainfall for the 2026 monsoon season, predicting just 90% of the long-period average. An El Niño pattern — characterised by warming of Pacific Ocean surface waters — is expected to suppress rainfall across much of South and Southeast Asia.

Government officials maintained that the lower target was "realistic" rather than reactionary, and said it was roughly in line with the previous year's initial target. But trade analysts were less sanguine.

## The Geopolitical Overlay

"Due to the current geopolitical tensions, the prediction of 90 per cent of normal rainfall is definitely a concern," a trade policy expert told The Hindu BusinessLine. "Though in some of the food items like rice and wheat India is comfortable due to previous year's surplus, several items including fruits and vegetables may be affected if the rainfall drops below 90 per cent, as spatial distribution is also predicted to be disrupted this year."

The geopolitical tensions the analyst referred to are not abstract. The Iran war has driven up global energy prices, which feed directly into the cost of fertilisers, transportation, and irrigation — the three pillars of Indian agriculture. Diesel-dependent farming operations face a double squeeze: weaker rains and costlier fuel.

## What India Has in Reserve

The country's wheat and rice buffer stocks remain comfortable. India ended the 2025-26 rabi season with surplus wheat procurement, and rice stocks from the previous kharif season provide a cushion. The government has already banned or restricted exports of several food commodities — including non-basmati rice — as a precautionary measure.

But the vulnerability lies in perishables. Fruits, vegetables, and pulses lack the strategic buffer that rice and wheat enjoy. A poor monsoon could trigger localised inflation spikes in these categories, particularly in states dependent on rain-fed agriculture like Maharashtra, Karnataka, and Madhya Pradesh.

## The NRI Kitchen Connection

For the Indian diaspora, food prices in India are never an abstraction. Remittances to families back home — totalling over $125 billion annually — absorb price shocks in everything from tur dal to onions. A bad monsoon year tends to accelerate remittance flows as families lean harder on their members abroad.

It also affects the global spice and grain trade. India is the world's largest producer of spices, pulses, and milk, and a top-three producer of rice and wheat. Export restrictions triggered by poor harvests ripple through grocery aisles from Edison to Southall.

The monsoon is expected to hit the Kerala coast in the first week of June. How it distributes rainfall across the Indo-Gangetic plain over the following eight weeks will determine whether the lower target was prudent planning or an underestimate of the challenge ahead.
author: Diaspora Desk
